content: Erysipelas is an acute inflammatory condition of the epidermis caused by bacterial infection. The primary causative agent is Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as group A streptococci. Other streptococcal groups, such as groups G, B, and C, can also cause erysipelas. Rarely, the condition may be caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae. The disease is characterized by a distinct rash localized to the epidermis. Clinical signs include erythema (redness), edema (swelling), bullae (large blisters), vesicles (small blisters), and blebs (fluid-filled lesions). Erysipelas most commonly affects the legs but can also appear on the face, torso, hands, feet, and toes. Patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, fatigue, headaches, vomiting, and pain, along with redness and swelling in the affected area. The onset of erysipelas typically occurs shortly after a streptococcal infection. Initial symptoms include localized lesions with erythema and edema. The condition progresses rapidly from the initial site, with raised and sharply demarcated boundaries separating the affected area from surrounding healthy tissue. Systemic symptoms, including fever, chills, and vomiting, may develop as the inflammation persists and spreads. Erysipelas must be distinguished from other inflammatory dermatological conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as pain, erythema, edema, and blisters, as well as systemic symptoms like fever, chills, fatigue, headache, and vomiting. Risk factors for erysipelas include conditions that predispose individuals to an inflammatory reaction to streptococcal infection. These include immunocompromised states, obesity, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, multiple deep skin lesions or ulcers, and disruptions to the cutaneous barrier. The cornerstone of erysipelas treatment is antimicrobial therapy. Pharmacologic options include penicillins, erythromycin, or cephalosporins. For facial erysipelas, empiric therapy may involve vancomycin, daptomycin, or linezolid. Surgery is not typically recommended but may be necessary in cases of severe complications, such as tissue necrosis or suppuration. Primary prevention of erysipelas involves measures to prevent streptococcal infections and their subsequent pathogenesis. Secondary prevention focuses on antibiotic prophylaxis for severe cases with a high recurrence rate. Agents such as phenoxymethylpenicillin, erythromycin, and benzathine penicillin have shown varying levels of efficacy in preventing recurrence. Further research is needed to standardize antibiotic selection, dosing, and administration intervals for universal application. Without treatment, the prognosis of erysipelas depends on the presence of complications. If the infection spreads below the dermis, it can lead to hospitalization and potentially life-threatening conditions. Complications may include the spread of infection to the bloodstream, brain, bones, kidneys, and other subcutaneous tissues. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is favorable, and penicillin has been shown to effectively relieve symptoms and halt disease progression. Historically, erysipelas was known as St. Anthony's Fire. The causative agent, Streptococcus bacteria, was identified by German physician Wilhelm Busch in 1881. Treatment development began in 1882 when Louis Pasteur discovered the attenuating effects of rabbits on Streptococcus. In 1944, scientists Fortner and Dinter published research on the efficacy of the first erysipelas vaccine, paving the way for further vaccine development. Erysipelas develops when streptococcal bacteria penetrate the epidermis, often through abrasions or lesions that allow the pathogen to adhere to the skin. The bacteria express virulence factors, such as M protein or fibronectin-binding protein, which facilitate invasion and inhibit phagocytosis. The inflammatory response, driven by an increased volume of leukocytes and the release of streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins, leads to tissue damage characteristic of erysipelas. Genetic predisposition and susceptibility to group A streptococcal infections may also play a role. Epidemiological data on erysipelas are limited. A 2004 study in Belgium estimated an incidence of 249 cases per 100,000 individuals in Europe. The condition primarily affects individuals over 50 years of age, with a median age of 55–60 years. Gender predominance is inconclusive, as studies have shown varying results regarding male and female prevalence. There is no diagnostic classification scheme or screening procedure for erysipelas. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical history and physical examination. Laboratory tests are not routinely performed but may be used to confirm streptococcal infection. Markers of inflammation, such as leukocytosis, may be present. Imaging studies, including X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds, are not diagnostic for erysipelas. In summary, erysipelas is a bacterial skin infection requiring prompt recognition and treatment to prevent complications. Antimicrobial therapy remains the mainstay of management, and prevention strategies focus on reducing the risk of streptococcal infections and recurrence.
